subject: Accounting
title: Step Costs
description: A short lesson to help you apply Step Costs.

hook.text: A call center handles 500 calls per agent. At 501 calls, you need another agent—costs jump.

buildup.text: Step costs stay flat within a range but jump to a new level when capacity is exceeded.

discovery.text: Hiring staff, renting warehouse space, and buying machines all create step-cost patterns.

twist.text: Right after a step increase, each unit costs much more—until volume fills the new capacity.

climax.text: Smart managers time growth to stay near the top of each step—maximizing use of paid capacity.

punchline.text: Costs don't always climb gradually. Sometimes they jump.

quiz.question: What are step costs?
options: Costs that stay flat then jump at capacity limits
Costs that increase with every unit

details.summary: Step costs remain fixed over a range of activity but jump to a new level when a threshold is crossed—like needing an additional supervisor after reaching a certain headcount. This topic explains how step costs behave, why they're tricky to predict, and how to plan for them.
details.whyItMatters: Step costs look fixed until they suddenly aren't. Failing to anticipate these jumps leads to budget surprises and inaccurate cost predictions at critical production thresholds.
takeaways: Step costs stay constant within a range but increase in steps when activity exceeds specific thresholds
Narrow-step costs (changing with small volume changes) may be treated as variable for planning
Wide-step costs (changing only with large volume shifts) are treated as fixed within the relevant range

faq.question: What is a step cost?
faq.answer: A step cost stays constant over a range of activity but jumps to a higher level once a threshold is reached. For example, one quality inspector can handle 1,000 units per shift; at 1,001 units, you need a second inspector and costs jump by an entire salary.

faq.question: How do you budget for step costs?
faq.answer: Identify the activity thresholds where each step occurs and estimate how many steps you'll need at your planned volume. Build budget scenarios for volumes near step boundaries so you're prepared for potential cost increases.
